title: United 232 at Sioux City
text:
On 19 July 1989 United Airlines Flight 232, a DC-10 flying from Denver to Chicago with 296 people aboard, suffered an explosive failure of its tail engine. Debris cut through all three hydraulic systems. The pilots had lost the normal use of their flight controls: no ailerons, no rudder, no elevators.

Captain Al Haynes, First Officer William Records and Flight Engineer Dudley Dvorak found that they could only steer by changing the thrust of the two remaining wing engines. A DC-10 training captain traveling as a passenger, Dennis Fitch, came forward to offer help. Haynes gave him the throttles, and Fitch knelt between the seats working them while the others handled the yoke, the radio and the checklists. For about forty minutes the four men shared information constantly, talked through every option, and nursed the plane toward Sioux City. When the controller cleared them to land on any runway, Haynes laughed and asked, "You want to be particular and make it a runway, huh?"

The plane hit the runway hard, broke apart and burst into flames. One hundred and twelve people died, but 184 survived, many helped by local emergency services that had rehearsed a similar disaster.

Investigators found that the crew had done remarkably well with an aircraft that was nearly impossible to fly. Haynes later credited his airline's crew resource management training, which had taught captains to draw on everyone in the cockpit rather than command alone.
lesson: In a crisis, a leader who shares the problem and uses everyone's skills gets far more than one who tries to carry it alone. Training to work together pays off when it matters most.
people: Al Haynes, Dennis Fitch, William Records, Dudley Dvorak
source: National Transportation Safety Board, Aircraft Accident Report NTSB/AAR-90/06 (1990)
place: Sioux Gateway Airport, Sioux City, Iowa
